items.prompt: What does an amortized O(1) operation guarantee?

options.text: For every allowed operation sequence, total cost divided across the sequence is O(1) per operation, even if some individual operations are expensive.
Every individual operation has worst-case O(1) cost.
The expected cost is O(1) only under a random input distribution.
Only the first operation is O(1).

feedback.reason: Amortized O(1) bounds the total cost of an operation sequence by O(m) for m operations; it does not bound every individual call by O(1).

blocks.text: Read the claim at sequence level

Let cᵢ be the actual cost of operation i. An amortized O(1) guarantee means that for every valid sequence of m operations, c₁ + c₂ + … + cₘ is O(m). Dividing that total by m gives constant amortized cost, even if one cᵢ is much larger than a constant.

blocks.title: Concrete example
blocks.text: Nine appends may cost 1 unit each and the tenth may cost 11 because it resizes. The total is 20 for 10 appends, so the sequence still averages 2 units per append; the tenth append itself was not constant-cost.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.each_worst_constant: This replaces a sequence-total guarantee with a per-call latency guarantee. A resize, cleanup, or rebuild may still make one operation O(n).
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.random_average: That is average-case or expected analysis because it depends on a probability distribution. Amortized analysis can bound every allowed operation sequence without randomness.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.first_only: The first operation has no special status. The guarantee relates the total charged work to the number of operations across the whole sequence.

items.prompt: How does amortized analysis differ from average-case analysis?

options.text: Amortized analysis does not require a probability distribution over inputs or operations.
They are identical names for the same concept.
Amortized analysis is the worst-case cost of one operation.
Amortized analysis applies only to output size.

feedback.reason: Average-case analysis takes an expectation over a stated probability model; amortized analysis bounds the aggregate cost of every valid sequence.

blocks.text: Separate the quantifiers

items: Average case: choose a distribution over inputs or operations, then compute expected cost under that model.
Amortized case: take any valid sequence, bound its total cost, then distribute that bound across the operations.

blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
blocks.text: A binary counter has an amortized constant number of bit flips over any sequence of increments; no random counter values are required. Conversely, an expected hash-table bound depends on assumptions about hashing and keys, so it is not automatically an amortized proof.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same: Average case depends on a distribution; amortized analysis can hold for every sequence.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.worst_each: Worst-case cost asks how expensive one operation can be. Amortized cost instead bounds the aggregate work of a sequence and may allow an expensive call.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.output_only: Amortized analysis applies to repeated operations such as append, increment, or multipop. Output size is relevant only when it contributes to the chosen cost model.

items.prompt: A dynamic array doubles capacity when full. What are the worst-case and amortized costs of one append under the fixed-element-copy model?

options.text: Worst-case O(n), amortized O(1).
Both worst-case and amortized O(1).
Both O(n).
Worst-case O(1), amortized O(n).

feedback.reason: A resize can copy n existing elements in one call, but geometric growth keeps the sum of all copies across n appends in O(n).

blocks.text: Derive both bounds

items: Worst case for one append: when the array is full, allocate a larger buffer and copy all n stored elements, so that call costs O(n).
Aggregate cost for n appends: resize copies have sizes 1, 2, 4, 8, …, whose sum is below 2n.
Add n ordinary writes: total work remains O(n), and O(n) divided across n appends is O(1) amortized.

blocks.title: Keep the two questions separate
blocks.text: Use the largest single resize for the worst-case bound and the geometric sum of every resize for the amortized bound.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.both_1: Ordinary appends are constant-cost, but an append that fills the buffer may copy all n existing elements, so its worst case is not O(1).
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.both_n: The O(n) copy happens only at geometrically spaced capacities. Most appends perform one write, and all resize copies together remain linear.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.worst_1_amortized_n: This reverses the contracts: a single resize can be linear, while distributing the linear sequence total across n appends gives constant amortized cost.

items.prompt: A dynamic array doubles its capacity when full. Why does this make append amortized O(1)?

options.text: Each resize leaves proportionally more free slots, so the next expensive copy comes only after many cheap appends.
It eliminates copying entirely.
It makes resize positions random.
The variable capacity has a special Big-O meaning.

feedback.reason: Across n appends, doubling copies fewer than 2n elements in total, so the total copying cost is O(n).

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Suppose capacities grow 1 → 2 → 4 → 8. The resizes copy 1, then 2, then 4 elements, but each resize is followed by enough cheap appends to fill the new free slots. After n appends, the total number of copied elements is 1 + 2 + 4 + … < 2n. Adding the n ordinary writes still gives O(n) total work, which is O(1) amortized per append.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: The conclusion is about a sequence: n appends cost O(n) in total. One append that triggers a resize can still cost O(n). If capacity grew by only one slot, the copies would sum to 1 + 2 + … + n = Θ(n²), so append would be Θ(n) amortized instead.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.copy_never: Doubling does not eliminate copying; it makes resize events sparse enough that their total copy cost stays linear.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.randomness: Resize positions are deterministic: they occur when sizes reach the current capacities 1, 2, 4, 8, and so on.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.names: The bound comes from the multiplicative growth rule and the resulting geometric sum, not from the variable name.

items.prompt: A stack supports push, pop, and multipop(k), where multipop removes at most k existing items. Why can multipop be amortized O(1) over a sequence?

options.text: Each pushed item can be popped at most once before it would need to be pushed again.
Every multipop call removes at most one item.
The stack remains sorted.
k is chosen randomly.

feedback.reason: The total number of successful pops is bounded by the total number of pushes.

blocks.text: Charge each removal once

Give each pushed item one credit that pays for its eventual removal. A multipop may remove many items in one call, but it can spend only credits created by earlier pushes. Once an item is removed, it cannot be charged again unless a later push inserts it as a new stack occurrence.

blocks.title: Sequence bound
blocks.text: Across m total stack operations there are at most m pushes and therefore at most m successful removals. Push overhead plus all removals is O(m), so the amortized cost per operation is O(1), even though one multipop may be O(m).

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.multipop_constant: A single multipop(k) can remove up to k existing items and can therefore be expensive. The bound comes from limiting total removals across the sequence.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.stack_sorted: LIFO order does not bound the number of removals. The decisive resource is that each pushed occurrence can be removed at most once.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.random_k: The proof works for every legal sequence of k values. It uses the push/pop accounting invariant, not a probability distribution.

items.prompt: A binary counter increments by flipping trailing ones to zero and the next zero to one. Why is increment amortized O(1) bit flips?

options.text: Higher bits flip exponentially less often, so total flips over n increments are O(n).
Every increment flips exactly one bit.
The claim holds only because the counter width is one bit.
Bit patterns are assumed random.

feedback.reason: Bit k flips once every 2ᵏ increments, so the total flip count forms a geometric series below 2n over n increments.

blocks.text: Count flips by bit position

items: Bit 0 flips on every increment: at most n flips.
Bit 1 flips every 2 increments: at most n/2 flips.
Bit 2 flips every 4 increments: at most n/4 flips; higher bits continue the same pattern.
The total is n + n/2 + n/4 + … < 2n, so n increments perform O(n) bit flips.

blocks.title: One increment can still be expensive
blocks.text: Incrementing 0111…111 flips every trailing 1 and then the next 0, so that call costs Θ(log n) flips for values up to n. The linear sequence total, not a one-flip-per-call claim, yields O(1) amortized cost.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.every_increment_one_flip: An increment such as 0111 → 1000 flips four bits. Cheap increments are more frequent, but not every increment flips exactly one bit.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.counter_width_constant_only: The geometric-frequency argument includes every bit position that appears as the counter grows; it does not assume a one-bit counter.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.random_bits: The flip schedule follows deterministically from binary carries. The geometric sum holds without assuming random counter values.

items.prompt: Can an amortized O(1) operation still cause a visible latency spike in one call?

options.text: Yes. Amortized analysis permits occasional expensive individual operations.
No. Amortized O(1) means strict worst-case O(1).
Only under random inputs.
Only when output size is large.

feedback.reason: Amortized O(1) constrains aggregate throughput, while a single resize, rebuild, or cleanup may still have a larger worst-case latency.

blocks.text: Throughput is not a latency ceiling

Suppose 99 calls cost 1 ms and one rebuild costs 101 ms. The total is 200 ms for 100 calls, so the amortized cost is 2 ms, but one caller still waits 101 ms. Amortization moves cost across calls for analysis; it does not make the expensive work disappear from the call that performs it.

blocks.title: Choose the guarantee from the requirement
blocks.text: Use amortized bounds for sustained sequence cost. If a deadline, frame budget, or real-time response must hold for every call, require a per-operation worst-case bound or schedule the expensive work explicitly.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.no: This treats an aggregate bound as a per-call bound. An occasional O(n) resize is compatible with O(1) amortized append.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.only_random: The expensive event can occur at deterministic states, such as exactly when a dynamic array reaches capacity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.only_output: A call may resize storage, rebuild an index, or perform cleanup even when it returns a constant-size result.

items.prompt: Is the statement "an operation is usually cheap" sufficient to prove a good amortized bound?

options.text: No. The frequency and total cost of expensive operations must be bounded over every valid sequence.
Yes. Informal frequency is enough.
Yes, because amortized means probabilistic.
Only the operation name is needed.

feedback.reason: “Usually cheap” gives no bound on the number or total cost of expensive events; an amortized proof must account for every event in every valid sequence.

blocks.text: Replace frequency language with an accounting bound

For m operations, identify what pays for each expensive event. The aggregate method sums all actual costs; the accounting method assigns credits to cheap calls; the potential method proves that stored potential decreases when expensive work occurs. Each method must end with an O(m) total, not an informal claim about what happens most often.

blocks.title: Usually cheap can still be bad
blocks.text: If m − 1 calls cost 1 but the last call costs 2ᵐ, the operation is usually cheap yet the sequence total is exponential. Frequency alone says nothing until the expensive cost is also bounded.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.yes_usually: A rare event can dominate the entire sequence if its cost grows too quickly. Both its frequency and total charge require a bound.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.yes_random: Amortized analysis can prove a bound for every valid sequence. A probabilistic claim instead needs an explicit distribution and expectation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.names: An operation name contains no cost model, event frequency, or sequence invariant, so it cannot establish an amortized bound.

items.prompt: A data structure advertises amortized O(1) insertion. Which statement is safe?

options.text: A sequence of n insertions has O(n) total insertion cost under the stated model.
Every insertion individually takes O(1) worst-case time.
The guarantee holds only in expectation over random insertions.
Any preprocessing cost can be ignored.

feedback.reason: An O(1) amortized insertion guarantee implies O(n) total insertion cost for any sequence of n insertions covered by the stated model.

blocks.text: Translate between per-operation and sequence bounds

If the amortized charge per insertion is at most a constant C, then n insertions have total charge at most Cn, which is O(n). The actual costs need not be even: some insertions may be cheap and a resize or rebuild may be expensive, as long as their combined cost stays within the linear sequence bound.

blocks.title: Respect the stated model
blocks.text: The guarantee covers the work included in the insertion contract. Initialization, resizing, collision behavior, or deferred cleanup cannot be ignored unless the model explicitly excludes them.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.each_constant: This converts an average charge over the sequence into a worst-case promise for each call. Occasional expensive insertions may still occur.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.expected_only: Amortized analysis does not inherently use random insertions. An expectation claim would require a separate probability model.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.preprocessing_free: Every relevant cost must be assigned by the operation model. A cost does not disappear merely because it is called preprocessing.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly distinguish amortized and worst-case cost? Select all that apply.

options.text: Worst-case operation cost bounds the most expensive individual call.
Amortized cost bounds total cost across a sequence.
Amortized O(1) proves every call is O(1).
Both claims require a defined operation and cost model.

feedback.reason: Worst-case cost bounds one call, amortized cost bounds a sequence total, and both statements are meaningful only under an explicit operation and cost model.

blocks.text: Check each contract independently

items: Worst-case operation cost asks for the largest cost of one legal call at input or state size n.
Amortized cost asks for a bound on the total cost of a legal operation sequence, divided across its calls.
Both require the analyst to define which operation, state size, and work are being counted.

blocks.title: Compatible claims
blocks.text: Dynamic-array append can be worst-case O(n) because one resize copies n elements and amortized O(1) because all resize copies across n appends sum to O(n). The two labels answer different questions and do not contradict each other.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.amortized_each: Amortized O(1) permits occasional expensive calls; proving every call O(1) would require a worst-case O(1) bound.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.worst_single: Worst-case cost is the per-operation ceiling needed when every call must meet a latency bound.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.amortized_sequence: Amortized cost accounts for expensive calls by bounding their total charge across the surrounding cheap calls.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.both_use_model: Without a defined operation, state size, and charged work, neither worst-case nor amortized notation has a precise meaning.

items.prompt: Which facts support the dynamic-array amortized append proof? Select all that apply.

options.text: Capacity grows by a constant factor greater than one.
A resize copies the current number of stored elements.
The total copied elements across growth steps form a geometric sum O(n).
Capacity increases by exactly one on every full append.

feedback.reason: The proof depends on both the resize cost and how often it occurs.

blocks.text: Both parts of the proof are necessary

If capacities are 1, 2, 4, 8, …, a resize copies the elements already stored. Before the array reaches size n, the copy work is 1 + 2 + 4 + …, which is less than 2n. Adding the n ordinary writes keeps the total work O(n), so n appends cost O(1) amortized each.

items: Geometric growth makes resize events increasingly far apart.
Copying the current elements defines the cost of each expensive event.
The geometric sum proves that all copies together are O(n).

blocks.title: Why growing by one fails
blocks.text: With capacities 1, 2, 3, …, the copies sum to 1 + 2 + … + (n − 1) = Θ(n²), so append becomes Θ(n) amortized rather than O(1).

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.grow_one: That would cause 1 + 2 + ... + n copying, which is quadratic.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.geometric_growth: A constant growth factor greater than one makes each new capacity cover a constant fraction more future appends before another resize.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.copy_existing: The resize cost is proportional to the current size because every stored element must be copied once.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.geometric_sum: Summing the copy sizes across all geometric growth steps gives O(n), which is the required aggregate bound.

items.prompt: Which methods can establish an amortized bound? Select all that apply.

options.text: Bound total cost of n operations and divide by n.
Charge extra credit to cheap operations to pay for later expensive ones.
Track stored potential whose change offsets actual cost.
Measure a random subset and call the average amortized.

feedback.reason: Amortized proofs can be presented through total cost, credits, or potential.

blocks.text: Three proof languages, one sequence bound

items: Aggregate: bound the actual cost T(n) of an arbitrary n-operation sequence, then use T(n) / n.
Accounting: assign each operation a charge; unused credit from cheap operations pays for later expensive work, and credit must never become negative.
Potential: choose a nonnegative state function Φ and analyze actual cost + Φ(after) − Φ(before); the potential change accounts for stored work.

blocks.title: What is not a proof
blocks.text: A measured average over a random sample depends on the sampled distribution. It does not establish the deterministic sequence guarantee supplied by any of the three amortized methods.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.random_sample: Sampling estimates behavior under the sampled distribution; it neither covers every valid operation sequence nor accounts for unsampled expensive events.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.aggregate: The aggregate method proves an upper bound on total actual cost and divides that bound across the operations.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.accounting: The accounting method gives cheap operations surplus credit and proves that the accumulated credit always covers later expensive operations.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.potential: The potential method represents prepaid work in the data structure state and includes the change in that stored potential in each amortized charge.

items.prompt: Which claims are invalid uses of amortized analysis? Select all that apply.

options.text: A real-time requirement can ignore a worst-case O(n) resize because append is amortized O(1).
A measured mean over random inputs is automatically an amortized proof.
An unbounded cleanup is harmless merely because it occurs rarely, without bounding rarity or cost.
n amortized-O(1) operations have O(n) total charged cost.

feedback.reason: Amortized analysis cannot replace latency guarantees or unproven frequency assumptions.

blocks.text: Test the claimed guarantee

items: A real-time deadline is a per-call requirement, so an occasional O(n) resize can violate it even when the sequence average is O(1).
A measured random-input mean is evidence about that distribution, not a proof for every valid sequence.
Calling cleanup rare is insufficient: both how often it can occur and how much it can cost must be bounded.

blocks.title: The valid implication
blocks.text: If the amortized charge is bounded by a constant C for n operations under the stated model, their total charged cost is at most Cn = O(n). This is a sequence claim, not a latency promise.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sequence_total: This is valid: multiplying the O(1) amortized charge by n operations gives an O(n) total charged cost under the same model.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.ignore_spike: Real-time latency requires a bound on every call; an amortized bound permits the very spike that the requirement forbids.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.random_average: A sample mean depends on the chosen distribution and cannot replace a bound over every valid sequence.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.unbounded_cleanup: Without a bound on frequency and cost, even one cleanup can dominate the total sequence cost.

elements.text: Define an arbitrary sequence of n allowed operations.
Bound the total actual cost of the whole sequence.
Divide the total bound by n.
State the amortized result and any separate worst-case operation cost.

feedback.reason: The aggregate method proves a sequence guarantee directly.

blocks.text: The proof must move from a sequence to a per-operation charge

items: Choose an arbitrary legal sequence of n operations so the proof is not tied to one favorable trace.
Count or upper-bound the actual work of the entire sequence, including every expensive event.
Divide that total bound by n to obtain the amortized cost per operation.
State the result together with any different worst-case cost of one operation.

blocks.title: Example conclusion
blocks.text: If n stack operations perform at most n pushes and n successful pops, total work is O(n); dividing by n gives O(1) amortized, while one multipop can still cost O(n).

items.prompt: Arrange an accounting-method explanation for dynamic-array append.

elements.text: Charge each cheap append a constant amount greater than its immediate cost.
Use accumulated credit to pay for the next resize copy.
Conclude a constant amortized charge covers every append.

feedback.reason: Credits move cost from rare expensive operations to preceding cheap operations.

blocks.text: Credits are prepaid work, not free work

items: Charge each ordinary append a fixed amount larger than its immediate unit write cost.
Keep the unused part as conceptual credit associated with stored elements or unused capacity.
When a resize copies existing elements, spend the accumulated credit on those copies.
Prove that every resize is fully funded and the credit balance never becomes negative; the fixed charge is then the amortized bound.

blocks.title: What the proof must show
blocks.text: Saying that cheap appends save credit is incomplete unless the chosen charge covers every later copy. A negative balance would mean the claimed amortized charge was too small.

items.prompt: A dynamic array starts empty and doubles capacity. Across n appends, select total append cost, amortized cost per append, and worst-case cost of one append.

feedback.reason: Geometric resize copies sum to O(n) across n appends.

blocks.text: Count the ordinary writes and resize copies separately

The n appends perform n ordinary element writes. With doubling, resize copies have sizes 1, 2, 4, … up to less than n, and their geometric sum is below 2n. Total work is therefore below a constant times n, so dividing by n gives O(1) amortized per append.

blocks.title: Keep the single-call bound separate
blocks.text: The append that triggers the largest resize copies Θ(n) existing elements, so its individual worst-case cost is O(n) even though the sequence total is O(n).

items.prompt: A stack executes m operations chosen from push, pop, and multipop. Each pushed item can be removed at most once before a later push. Select total cost and amortized cost per operation.
constraints: Each successful push or pop costs O(1).

feedback.reason: There can be at most m pushes and at most one successful pop per pushed item.

blocks.text: Charge each removal to the push that created the item

Across m operations there are at most m pushes. Once an item is successfully popped—whether by pop or multipop—it is gone and cannot be removed again without a new push. Charge that removal to its creating push: there are at most m successful removals plus O(m) operation overhead, so total cost is O(m).

blocks.title: Large call, linear sequence
blocks.text: After k pushes, one multipop(k) costs Θ(k), but those k removals cannot be charged again. Dividing the O(m) sequence total by m operations gives O(1) amortized, while one multipop remains O(m) worst case.

items.prompt: A binary counter starts at zero and is incremented n times. Select total bit flips, amortized flips per increment, and worst-case flips of one increment.
constraints: The counter has enough bits to represent values through n.

feedback.reason: Each bit flips at a geometrically decreasing frequency, so total flips are linear.

blocks.text: Sum flips by bit position

Over n increments, bit 0 flips on every increment, bit 1 on about every second, bit 2 on about every fourth, and so on. The total is at most n + n/2 + n/4 + … < 2n = O(n), so the amortized number of flips is O(1).

blocks.title: Worst-case increment
blocks.text: Incrementing a value such as 011…111 clears every trailing one and sets the next zero. A counter representing values through n has Θ(log n) bits, so one increment may flip O(log n) bits.
